claim: Hippocampal-dependent memory is thought to be supported by distinct connectivity states, with strong input to the hippocampus benefitting encoding and weak input benefitting retrieval.
source: Hippocampal-dependent memory is thought to be supported by distinct connectivity states, with strong input to the hippocampus benefitting encoding and weak input benefitting retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific literature on hippocampal connectivity states and memory processes.

claim: In rodents, the hippocampal theta oscillation orchestrates the transition between distinct connectivity states.
source: Previous research in rodents suggests that the hippocampal theta oscillation orchestrates the transition between these states, with opposite phase angles predicting minimal versus maximal input.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior rodent research on theta oscillations and connectivity.

claim: Opposite theta phase angles predict minimal versus maximal input to the hippocampus in rodents.
source: Previous research in rodents suggests that the hippocampal theta oscillation orchestrates the transition between these states, with opposite phase angles predicting minimal versus maximal input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies on theta phase and hippocampal input.

claim: Lateral temporal stimulation evoked ipsilateral hippocampal potentials with distinct early and late components.
source: Lateral temporal stimulation evoked ipsilateral hippocampal potentials with distinct early and late components.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the study showing evoked potentials.

claim: The maximal difference in evoked component amplitudes occurred across 180 degrees of separation in the hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: The maximal difference in these evoked component amplitudes occurred across 180 degrees of separation in the hippocampal theta rhythm; that is, the greatest difference in component amplitude was observed when stimulation was delivered at theta peak versus trough.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing phase-dependent amplitude differences.

claim: The greatest difference in component amplitude was observed when stimulation was delivered at theta peak versus trough.
source: The maximal difference in these evoked component amplitudes occurred across 180 degrees of separation in the hippocampal theta rhythm; that is, the greatest difference in component amplitude was observed when stimulation was delivered at theta peak versus trough.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing peak and trough stimulation.

claim: The pattern of theta-phase dependence observed for hippocampus was not identified for control locations.
source: The pattern of theta-phase dependence observed for hippocampus was not identified for control locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from control region analyses.

claim: Hippocampal receptivity to input varies with theta phase.
source: These findings demonstrate that hippocampal receptivity to input varies with theta phase, suggesting that theta phase reflects connectivity states of human hippocampal networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings of phase-dependent responses.

claim: Theta phase reflects connectivity states of human hippocampal networks.
source: These findings demonstrate that hippocampal receptivity to input varies with theta phase, suggesting that theta phase reflects connectivity states of human hippocampal networks.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing phase-dependent connectivity.

claim: Memory formation benefits from increased input via connectivity of entorhinal cortex to CA1.
source: This process is thought to benefit from increased input via connectivity of entorhinal cortex to CA1 (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Maass et al., 2014; Brankack et al., 1993; Kamondi et al., 1998; Fernández et al., 1999) along with reduced recurrent hippocampal connectivity (Hasselmo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on hippocampal connectivity during memory formation.

claim: Memory formation benefits from reduced recurrent hippocampal connectivity.
source: This process is thought to benefit from increased input via connectivity of entorhinal cortex to CA1 (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Maass et al., 2014; Brankack et al., 1993; Kamondi et al., 1998; Fernández et al., 1999) along with reduced recurrent hippocampal connectivity (Hasselmo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hasselmo et al., 2002.

claim: Retrieval involves hippocampal-dependent reactivation.
source: Retrieval involves hippocampal-dependent reactivation (Waldhauser et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Tayler et al., 2013; Eichenbaum, 2000), which is thought to benefit from the opposite functional connectivity pattern (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Duncan et al., 2014; Montgomery and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to research on hippocampal reactivation during retrieval.

claim: Retrieval benefits from the opposite functional connectivity pattern compared to encoding.
source: Retrieval involves hippocampal-dependent reactivation (Waldhauser et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2014; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Tayler et al., 2013; Eichenbaum, 2000), which is thought to benefit from the opposite functional connectivity pattern (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Duncan et al., 2014; Montgomery and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on connectivity patterns during retrieval.

claim: Rodent hippocampal theta synchrony supports memory formation and retrieval.
source: Rodent hippocampal theta synchrony supports memory formation and retrieval (Markowska et al., 1995; Winson, 1978), with different theta phases thought to support opposing functional connectivity patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies on theta and memory.

claim: Different theta phases support opposing functional connectivity patterns in rodents.
source: Rodent hippocampal theta synchrony supports memory formation and retrieval (Markowska et al., 1995; Winson, 1978), with different theta phases thought to support opposing functional connectivity patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and established knowledge about theta phase and connectivity.

claim: Tetanic electrical stimulation of hippocampal CA1 results in long-term potentiation when delivered at the stratum radiatum theta peak.
source: For instance, tetanic electrical stimulation of hippocampal CA1 results in long-term potentiation when delivered at the stratum radiatum theta peak versus long-term depression when delivered at the trough (Hölscher et al., 1997; Hyman et al., 2003), supporting a theta-phase dependence of encoding readiness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hölscher et al., 1997 and Hyman et al., 2003.

claim: Tetanic electrical stimulation of hippocampal CA1 results in long-term depression when delivered at the trough.
source: For instance, tetanic electrical stimulation of hippocampal CA1 results in long-term potentiation when delivered at the stratum radiatum theta peak versus long-term depression when delivered at the trough (Hölscher et al., 1997; Hyman et al., 2003), supporting a theta-phase dependence of encoding readiness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hölscher et al., 1997 and Hyman et al., 2003.

claim: Disrupting the theta cycle with inhibitory stimulation locked to local peak versus trough differentially impacts encoding and retrieval in rodents.
source: In addition, disrupting the theta cycle with inhibitory stimulation locked to local peak versus trough has been shown to differentially impact encoding and retrieval in rodents (Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Siegle and Wilson, 2014.

claim: Human hippocampal theta characteristics differ from rodent hippocampal theta, including the presence and functional relevance of high-power oscillatory bouts.
source: It is currently unclear whether human hippocampus shows the phase dependence of receptivity to external input that has been identified in rodents, particularly given the numerous differences in human versus rodent hippocampal theta characteristics including the presence and functional relevance of high-power oscillatory bouts (Goyal et al., 2020; Jacobs, 2014; Kahana et al., 1999; Raghavachari et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on human versus rodent theta characteristics.

claim: Lateral temporal cortex has putative projections to entorhinal cortex and hippocampus.
source: We applied direct electrical stimulation to hippocampal network sites in lateral temporal cortex with putative projections to entorhinal cortex and hippocampus (Insausti et al., 1987; Catani and Thiebaut de Schotten, 2008; Zhong and Rockland, 2004), and measured the hippocampal response to lateral temporal stimulation using well-characterized early and late evoked-potential components (Matsumoto et al., 2004; Novitskaya et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Early and late evoked-potential components are well-characterized measures of hippocampal response to stimulation.
source: We applied direct electrical stimulation to hippocampal network sites in lateral temporal cortex with putative projections to entorhinal cortex and hippocampus (Insausti et al., 1987; Catani and Thiebaut de Schotten, 2008; Zhong and Rockland, 2004), and measured the hippocampal response to lateral temporal stimulation using well-characterized early and late evoked-potential components (Matsumoto et al., 2004; Novitskaya et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matsumoto et al., 2004 and Novitskaya et al., 2020.

claim: In rodents, fissural theta trough versus peak are the phases commonly related to maximal versus minimal receptivity to external input.
source: In rodents, fissural theta trough versus peak are the phases commonly related to maximal versus minimal receptivity to external input (e.g., Hasselmo, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hasselmo, 2005.

claim: The theta oscillation arises from interlaminar dipoles.
source: Because the theta oscillation arises from interlaminar dipoles (Goutagny et al., 2009; Kamondi et al., 1998), its observed phase varies according to electrode depth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goutagny et al., 2009 and Kamondi et al., 1998.

claim: Theta oscillation phase varies according to electrode depth.
source: Because the theta oscillation arises from interlaminar dipoles (Goutagny et al., 2009; Kamondi et al., 1998), its observed phase varies according to electrode depth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and knowledge about interlaminar dipoles.

claim: Data were collected from eight individuals with refractory epilepsy.
source: Data were collected from eight individuals with refractory epilepsy (two males; mean age ± standard deviation [SD]: 37 ± 10 years; range 28–55 years; Table 1) undergoing invasive electrophysiological monitoring as part of their inpatient clinical care at the Northwestern Memorial Hospital Comprehensive Epilepsy Center.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the methods section describing the participant sample.

claim: The participant sample included two males with mean age 37 ± 10 years (range 28–55 years).
source: Data were collected from eight individuals with refractory epilepsy (two males; mean age ± standard deviation [SD]: 37 ± 10 years; range 28–55 years; Table 1) undergoing invasive electrophysiological monitoring as part of their inpatient clinical care at the Northwestern Memorial Hospital Comprehensive Epilepsy Center.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the participant description.

claim: All participants had stereotactic EEG depth macroelectrodes implanted in hippocampus, amygdala, lateral temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex.
source: All participants had stereotactic EEG (sEEG) depth macroelectrodes (Ad-Tech, Oak Creek, WI) implanted in hippocampus, amygdala, lateral temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex, in addition to other regions.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the methods section.

claim: All stimulating electrodes were localized to lateral temporal cortex and adjacent white matter.
source: All stimulating electrodes were localized to lateral temporal cortex and adjacent white matter (Figure 1a, b; see Figure 1—animation 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the text and referenced figures showing electrode locations.

claim: Stimulation did not elicit seizure or clinically significant afterdischarges in any participant.
source: Stimulation did not elicit seizure or clinically significant afterdischarges in any participant.
evidence: This claim is directly stated as an observation from the experimental protocol.

claim: All analyzed hippocampal recording electrodes showed at least one narrowband oscillation in the 3–8 Hz range.
source: All analyzed hippocampal recording electrodes (as well as all amygdala and OFC control region recording electrodes) showed at least one narrowband oscillation in the 3–8 Hz range.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spectral analysis data presented in the results.

claim: All amygdala and OFC control region recording electrodes showed at least one narrowband oscillation in the 3–8 Hz range.
source: All analyzed hippocampal recording electrodes (as well as all amygdala and OFC control region recording electrodes) showed at least one narrowband oscillation in the 3–8 Hz range.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spectral analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Peaks where power was significantly greater than the 1/f background spectrum across electrodes were detected within the 3–8 Hz theta range at 5.3 and 6.3 Hz.
source: Peaks where power was significantly greater than the 1/f background spectrum across electrodes were detected within the 3–8 Hz theta range at 5.3 and 6.3 Hz (t-test of corrected power versus 0, 5.3 Hz: t(22) = 3.4, p = 0.003; 6.3 Hz: t(22) = 3.3, p = 0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spectral power data.

claim: Hippocampal evoked-potential components were estimated to occur from 27 to 113 ms (early) and 114 to 208 ms (late) post-stimulation.
source: Hippocampal evoked-potential (EP) components were estimated to occur from 27 to 113 ms (early) and 114 to 208 ms (late) post-stimulation (Figure 1d; see Materials and methods: Quantification of hippocampal EPs).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of evoked potentials shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The observed component latencies were consistent with values reported by previous studies of human hippocampal response to direct electrical stimulation of polysynaptic afferents.
source: The observed component latencies were consistent with values reported by previous studies of human hippocampal response to direct electrical stimulation of polysynaptic afferents (e.g., Kubota et al., 2013; Novitskaya et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited prior studies.

claim: Both early and late component amplitudes were significantly predicted by theta phase at stimulation onset.
source: Both early and late component amplitudes were significantly predicted by theta phase at stimulation onset (Figure 2a. Mean z-score ± SD, early: z = 1.3 ± 1.9; late: z = 1.2 ± 1.6. t-test of z-scores versus 0, early: t(22) = 3.3, p = 0.003, Cohen's d = 0.7; late: t(22) = 3.7, p = 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.8. Mean r ± SD, early: r = 0.080 ± 0.066; late: r = 0.076 ± 0.051).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of circular-linear correlations.

claim: Stimulation trials exhibited local increases in circular–linear correlation that coincided with the early and late EP components.
source: In contrast, stimulation trials exhibited local increases in circular–linear correlation (Figure 2c). Qualitatively, the local increases appeared to coincide with the early and late EP components (as plotted in Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the timecourse analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Peaks in the phase–amplitude relationship were found at +50 and +135 ms following stimulation onset, which aligns closely with the early and late EP components.
source: Using the same peak-finding method that identified peaks in the EP (see Materials and methods: Quantification of hippocampal EPs), we found peaks in the phase–amplitude relationship at +50 and +135 ms following stimulation onset, which aligns closely with the early and late EP components (+62 and +134 ms, respectively; Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by peak-finding analysis of the phase-amplitude relationship.

claim: The early and late EP components showed significant amplitude differences following peak versus trough stimulation.
source: The early and late EP components showed significant amplitude differences following peak versus trough stimulation (Figure 4a. Paired t-test across hippocampal recording electrodes, early: t(22) = −2.7, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = −0.2; late: t(22) = −2.6, p = 0.02, Cohen's d = −0.08. Mean peak − trough amplitude difference ± SD, early: diff = −4.9 ± 8.5 μV, diff = −3.9 ± 7.2 μV).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of peak and trough stimulation trials.

claim: The peak versus trough effect in the early component persisted through the isolation procedure.
source: However, the peak versus trough effect in the early component persisted through the isolation procedure (Figure 4b. Paired t-test: t(22) = −2.1, p = 0.05, Cohen's d = −0.2; mean amplitude difference ± SD, early: diff = −4.8 ± 11 μV; late: diff = −2.2 ± 10 μV).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the isolated evoked response.

claim: No difference in EP amplitude was observed for rising versus falling stimulation conditions for either early or late components.
source: No difference in EP amplitude was observed for rising versus falling stimulation conditions (Figure 3c) for either early or late components (Figure 4c. Paired t-test across hippocampal recording electrodes, early: t(22) = 0.45, p = 0.7, Cohen's d = 0.04; late: t(22) = 0.55, p = 0.6, Cohen's d = 0.03; mean falling − rising amplitude difference ± SD: early: diff = 1.1 ± 11.3 μV; late: diff = 1.6 ± 14.0 μV).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of rising and falling phase stimulation.

claim: In amygdala, stimulation EPs had distinct early and late negative components estimated to span 35–70 ms (early) and 94–256 ms (late).
source: In both control regions, stimulation EPs had distinct early and late negative components (Figure 5a, e). In amygdala, components were estimated to span 35–70 ms (early) and 94–256 ms (late).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of amygdala evoked potentials.

claim: In OFC, evoked potential components spanned 22–74 ms (early) and 74–490 ms (late).
source: In OFC, components spanned 22–74 ms (early) and 74–490 ms (late).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of OFC evoked potentials.

claim: Neither control region showed the clear, temporally specific increase in circular-linearity during the early component which was present in the hippocampal EP.
source: In contrast to the hippocampal EP (see Figure 2c), both control regions showed more diffuse deviations in the phase–amplitude relationship. In particular, neither control region showed the clear, temporally specific increase in circular-linearity during the early component which was present in the hippocampal EP.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of control region data to hippocampal data.

claim: The amygdala EP showed significant amplitude differences across peak and trough trials in the late component.
source: The amygdala EP showed significant amplitude differences across peak and trough trials in the late component (paired t-test: t(8) = −4.1, p = 0.003, Cohen's d = −0.2), with greater amplitude for peak trials (Figure 5c. Mean difference ± SD: −5.5 ± 4.0 μV).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of amygdala evoked potentials.

claim: There was no significant amplitude difference in the amygdala early component for peak versus trough stimulation.
source: There was no significant amplitude difference in the early component (t(8) = 0.85, p = 0.4, Cohen's d = 0.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of amygdala early component.

claim: For orbitofrontal EPs, no differences were found in either peak versus trough or rising versus falling trial amplitude in either early or late components.
source: In contrast, for orbitofrontal EPs, we found no differences in either peak versus trough or rising versus falling trial amplitude in either early or late components (Figure 5g, h. Peak versus trough, early: t(21) = 0.51, p = 0.6, Cohen's d = 0.04; late: t(21) = −0.77, p = 0.5, Cohen's d = −0.1. Rising versus falling, early: t(21) = −0.59, p = 0.6, Cohen's d = −0.04; late: t(21) = −0.08, p = 0.9, Cohen's d = −0.007).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of orbitofrontal evoked potentials.

claim: Across subjects, a positive phase–amplitude relationship was observed in both early and late components.
source: Across subjects, we observed a positive phase–amplitude relationship in both early and late components (mean z-score ± SD, early: z = 1.0 ± 1.3; late: z = 1.1 ± 1.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by subject-level analysis of phase-amplitude relationships.

claim: The phase-amplitude relationship effect was marginal across subjects in the early component and reached significance in the late component.
source: This effect was marginal across subjects in the early component and reached significance in the late component (t-test of z-scores versus 0, early: t(7) = 2.3, p = 0.06, Cohen's d = 0.8; late: t(7) = 2.8, p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 1.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing across subjects.

claim: Including the phase effect improved the linear mixed-effects model fit for the early component, with a marginal effect in the late component.
source: Including the phase effect improved the model fit for the early component, with a marginal effect in the late component (one-sided likelihood ratio test for improvement, early: LRStat = 3.8, p = 0.05; late: LRStat = 3.3, p = 0.06).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed-effects modeling results.

claim: Oscillatory synchronization (phase coupling) is a known mechanism that supports interregional communication.
source: Oscillatory synchronization (i.e., phase coupling) is a known mechanism that supports interregional communication (see Fries, 2005; Fell and Axmacher, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on oscillatory synchronization.

claim: Temporal lobe epilepsy is associated with episodic memory impairments.
source: Temporal lobe epilepsy is associated with episodic memory impairments (Mayeux et al., 1980; Helmstaedter and Kockelmann, 2006) thought to be caused by structural abnormalities as well as interictal epileptiform activity in the hippocampus and hippocampal cortical network (Helmstaedter and Kockelmann, 2006; Gelinas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on temporal lobe epilepsy and memory.

claim: Memory impairments in temporal lobe epilepsy are thought to be caused by structural abnormalities and interictal epileptiform activity in the hippocampus and hippocampal cortical network.
source: Temporal lobe epilepsy is associated with episodic memory impairments (Mayeux et al., 1980; Helmstaedter and Kockelmann, 2006) thought to be caused by structural abnormalities as well as interictal epileptiform activity in the hippocampus and hippocampal cortical network (Helmstaedter and Kockelmann, 2006; Gelinas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on mechanisms of memory impairment in epilepsy.

claim: Direct electrical stimulation of sensory cortices has been found to differentially induce long-term potentiation or depression depending on LFP phase.
source: Direct electrical stimulation of sensory cortices has been found to differentially induce long-term potentiation or depression depending on LFP phase e.g., with beta- and gamma-dependence in rodent visual cortex (Wespatat et al., 2004) and beta-dependence in primate sensorimotor cortex (Zanos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on phase-dependent plasticity in sensory cortices.

claim: Local oscillatory phase has been found to relate to the amplitude of the cortical response evoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation in humans.
source: In humans, local oscillatory phase has been found to relate to the amplitude of the cortical response evoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation (Kundu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kundu et al., 2014.

claim: Amygdala is physically adjacent to hippocampus and densely connected with hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.
source: But while amygdala is physically adjacent to hippocampus and densely connected with hippocampus and entorhinal cortex (Saunders et al., 1988; Pikkarainen et al., 1999; see Chrobak et al., 2000) – and might therefore be expected to show hippocampus-like phase dependence of input receptivity – orbitofrontal cortex is more distant both in space and connectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Orbitofrontal cortex is more distant from hippocampus both in space and connectivity compared to amygdala.
source: But while amygdala is physically adjacent to hippocampus and densely connected with hippocampus and entorhinal cortex (Saunders et al., 1988; Pikkarainen et al., 1999; see Chrobak et al., 2000) – and might therefore be expected to show hippocampus-like phase dependence of input receptivity – orbitofrontal cortex is more distant both in space and connectivity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from anatomical knowledge and the comparison to amygdala.

claim: The amygdala showed greater response amplitude when stimulation was applied at theta peak relative to trough.
source: As was the case in hippocampus, the amygdala showed greater response amplitude when stimulation was applied at theta peak relative to trough.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from amygdala analyses.

claim: The amygdala showed greater response amplitude to stimulation at theta rising phase relative to falling phase.
source: The amygdala also showed greater response amplitude to stimulation at theta rising phase relative to falling phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from amygdala analyses.

claim: The phase dependence effect in amygdala was present exclusively in the late component.
source: Unlike in hippocampus, this effect was present exclusively in the late component.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of early and late component results in amygdala.

claim: The presence of early components in the amygdala and orbitofrontal EPs supports connectivity between these control regions and the lateral temporal stimulation site.
source: The presence of early components in the amygdala and orbitofrontal EPs supports connectivity between these control regions and the lateral temporal stimulation site.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of evoked potentials in control regions.

claim: The stimulation site was chosen based on its functional connectivity with hippocampus as measured via the stimulation-evoked potential.
source: However, we note that the stimulation site was chosen on the basis of its functional connectivity with hippocampus as measured via the stimulation-evoked potential, and not based on connectivity with these other brain areas.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Hippocampal electrodes were implanted at variable laminar depths that could not be known due to the relative imprecision of CT/MRI.
source: As data in this study were collected opportunistically from participants undergoing clinically necessary invasive monitoring, hippocampal electrodes were implanted at variable laminar depths that could not be known due to the relative imprecision of CT/MRI.
evidence: This claim describes a limitation of the clinical electrode placement.

claim: The relatively small phase offset observed between hippocampal sites from a given participant supports that the recorded oscillation was depth indifferent.
source: The relatively small phase offset we observed between hippocampal sites from a given participant (see Appendix 1—figure 4) supports that the recorded oscillation was depth indifferent, perhaps owing to the large size and interlaminar placement of the macroelectrodes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phase offset data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The depth indifference of the recorded oscillation may be owing to the large size and interlaminar placement of the macroelectrodes.
source: The relatively small phase offset we observed between hippocampal sites from a given participant (see Appendix 1—figure 4) supports that the recorded oscillation was depth indifferent, perhaps owing to the large size and interlaminar placement of the macroelectrodes.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the cause of depth indifference.

claim: The observed effect of peak versus trough is likely specific to the synaptic distance and conduction delay between the stimulation site and hippocampus.
source: The observed effect of peak versus trough is likely specific to the synaptic distance and conduction delay between the stimulation site and hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about factors affecting the observed effects.

claim: Differences in transmission latencies may have contributed to the observed variance in peak–trough effects across participants.
source: It is possible that differences in transmission latencies contributed to the observed variance in peak–trough effects across participants.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about sources of variance.

claim: Stimulation targeting a different site in the hippocampal network would produce a similarly theta-periodic hippocampal response, albeit likely maximized at a different stimulation phase angle.
source: We hypothesize that stimulation targeting a different site in the hippocampal network would produce a similarly theta-periodic hippocampal response, albeit likely maximized at a different stimulation phase angle (i.e., not necessarily at the observed hippocampal theta peak).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how the findings would generalize to other stimulation sites.

claim: iEEG recordings from individuals with temporal lobe epilepsy have previously been used to study mechanisms for hippocampal function.
source: Nonetheless, iEEG recordings from individuals with temporal lobe epilepsy have previously been used to study mechanisms for hippocampal function (Lega et al., 2012; Long et al., 2014; Fell et al., 2011; Wixted et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies using epilepsy patient data.

claim: Trials with recorded epileptiform activity were rejected from the analysis.
source: To enhance the study's generalizability, we rejected trials with recorded epileptiform activity and ensured during data collection that the stimulation protocol did not elicit afterdischarges or spiking.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological step to control for epilepsy effects.

claim: Phase dependence of the response to stimulation has been demonstrated in non-epilepsy model organisms.
source: Phase dependence of the response to stimulation has, however, been demonstrated in non-epilepsy model organisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsequent citations to animal studies.

claim: Amygdala has anatomical and functional connectivity with the lateral temporal stimulation site.
source: Like hippocampus, both regions have anatomical (Shi and Cassell, 1997; Iwai et al., 1987; Morecraft et al., 1992) and functional (Roy et al., 2009; Du et al., 2020) connectivity with the lateral temporal stimulation site.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical and functional connectivity studies.

claim: Orbitofrontal cortex has anatomical and functional connectivity with the lateral temporal stimulation site.
source: Like hippocampus, both regions have anatomical (Shi and Cassell, 1997; Iwai et al., 1987; Morecraft et al., 1992) and functional (Roy et al., 2009; Du et al., 2020) connectivity with the lateral temporal stimulation site.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical and functional connectivity studies.

claim: In rodent CA1 depth penetrations, theta phase is stable through the strata oriens and pyramidale then undergoes a gradual phase shift, resulting in a 180° phase difference at the fissure compared to dorsal layers.
source: In depth penetrations of rodent CA1, theta phase is stable through the strata oriens and pyramidale then undergoes a gradual phase shift, resulting in a 180° phase difference at the fissure compared to dorsal layers (Brankack et al., 1993; Bragin et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent electrophysiology studies.

claim: Rodent hippocampal theta phase has been found to fully reverse between the longitudinal poles.
source: Rodent hippocampal theta phase has been found to fully reverse between the longitudinal poles (Patel et al., 2012) i.e., the 'traveling wave' model (Patel et al., 2012; Lubenov and Siapas, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on theta traveling waves.

claim: Monotonic phase shift across the long axis has been demonstrated to occur within individual CA subfields in rodents.
source: Monotonic phase shift across the long axis has also been demonstrated to occur within individual CA subfields (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lubenov and Siapas, 2009.

claim: In LFPs recorded along the human hippocampus via implanted depth electrodes, theta phase has been found to shift monotonically across the hippocampal long axis.
source: In LFPs recorded along the human hippocampus via implanted depth electrodes, theta phase has been found to shift monotonically across the hippocampal long axis (Zhang and Jacobs, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang and Jacobs, 2015.

claim: LFPs recorded from human depth electrodes generally reflect a sum of phase-asynchronous laminar inputs weighted by distance from the contributing layer to the electrode.
source: LFPs recorded from human depth electrodes generally reflect a sum of phase-asynchronous laminar inputs (West and Gundersen, 1990) weighted by distance from the contributing layer to the electrode.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to West and Gundersen, 1990 and general knowledge of LFP recording.

claim: The phase shift is stable across layers and septotemporal distance in hippocampus.
source: As the phase shift is stable across layers and septotemporal distance (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009), phase at a given electrode has a consistent offset to other hippocampal sites (Zhang and Jacobs, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on phase relationships in hippocampus.

claim: Phase at a given hippocampal electrode has a consistent offset to other hippocampal sites.
source: As the phase shift is stable across layers and septotemporal distance (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009), phase at a given electrode has a consistent offset to other hippocampal sites (Zhang and Jacobs, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang and Jacobs, 2015.
